topic: Coding Agents Without Handing Over Credentials
subtopic: Scoped access for agentic coding tools
hook: Most teams building with coding agents are stuck on the wrong question.
caption:
Most teams building with coding agents are stuck on the wrong question.

They ask what the agent can do. They should be asking what it can reach.

Right now a lot of agent setups work like this: give it a login, point it at the codebase, let it run. That means if the agent misfires, or gets prompted into doing something it shouldn't, it's acting with your full account permissions. Not a slice of them. All of them.

Several infrastructure and security teams have been writing about this lately, and they're converging on the same fix. Don't hand agents your credentials. Give them narrow, short-lived, revocable access scoped to exactly the task in front of them. A proxy or token that can do one job and expire, not a key that opens everything.

It's the same logic you'd apply to a new contractor. You don't give them the master key on day one. You give them access to the room they're working in.

The interesting part is that this isn't a model problem. GPT-5, Claude, whatever comes next, none of that changes the exposure. The exposure comes from how the agent is wired into your systems.

That's the part nobody wants to spend time on, because it's not flashy. But it's the difference between an agent that's useful and an agent that's a liability waiting for the wrong prompt.

If you're running agents against real accounts, the question worth asking isn't "what can this do." It's "what happens if this goes wrong, and what does it have access to when it does."

topic: Automation monitoring and silent failure
hook: Automation without monitoring is just a slower way to fail
caption:
Most automations don't fail loudly.

They fail quietly.

A workflow breaks on a Tuesday.
Nobody notices until Friday.
By then the CRM has bad data, the follow-up never went out, and someone is asking why a lead went cold.

Here's the part people skip when they build automations.

They build the happy path.
Form fills out correctly, API responds fast, data lands where it should.

They don't build for the version where the API times out, the field is empty, or the token expired.

A workflow that runs without errors in testing is not the same as a workflow that runs reliably for six months.

The second one needs logging.
It needs alerts when something breaks.
It needs a person who gets a message that says "this step failed" instead of finding out from a client.

The automation isn't the hard part anymore.
Watching it is.

What's one automation in your business that you'd actually know about if it silently broke tomorrow?

topic: Code Review Becomes the New Bottleneck
subtopic: AI coding agents shift workload downstream
hook: New Harvard research getting traction on Hacker News this week challenges a simple assumption: that faster code generation means faster shipping.
caption:
New Harvard research is getting traction on Hacker News this week, and it challenges a simple assumption: that faster code generation means faster shipping.

The finding is that as AI coding agents produce more code, the bottleneck in software teams shifts downstream to code review.

Think about what that means for how teams are structured right now.

Writing code used to be the expensive step. Review was the quick check before merge. If agents can write a feature in minutes, the team's real constraint becomes how fast a human can read, verify, and trust that output.

This is the same pattern I see when I design agent workflows for businesses. The model doing the work is rarely the hard part. The hard part is building the checkpoints around it: what gets reviewed, by whom, under what conditions, and what gets flagged instead of auto-approved.

Skip that design work and faster output just means a faster pile-up at the review stage.

If you're running coding agents on your team, where is the actual bottleneck now? Writing, reviewing, or deciding what even needs a human to look at it?

topic: Automation monitoring and silent failures
hook: Automation without monitoring is just a faster way to fail
caption:
Most automations fail quietly.

No error message.
No alert.
Just wrong data sitting in your CRM for three weeks before anyone notices.

Here's the part people skip when they build their first workflow.

They focus on the happy path.

Form fills out correctly.
API responds the way it should.
Data lands where it's supposed to.

Then one API changes a field name.
Or a rate limit kicks in.
Or a lead fills in their email wrong.

And the workflow doesn't crash.

It just keeps running, quietly producing garbage, because nobody built in a way to catch it.

The fix isn't more automation.

It's a simple layer most people treat as optional:

Logging what happened.
Flagging what looks off.
Alerting a real person when something breaks the pattern.

That's the unglamorous 20 percent of the build.

It's also the only part that makes the other 80 percent trustworthy.

What's the last automation you built that broke without telling you?

topic: Code Review Is The New Automation Bottleneck
subtopic: AI coding agents shift workload from writing to reviewing
hook: A team can now generate a pull request in minutes. Checking that pull request still takes the same amount of time it always did.
caption:
A team can now generate a pull request in minutes. Checking that pull request still takes the same amount of time it always did.

That gap just got attention. Harvard research on code review and AI-generated code surfaced on Hacker News this week, with a lot of people arguing about where the real bottleneck sits.

The finding lines up with something worth saying plainly: writing code was never the slow part for most teams. Reading it, tracing what it touches, deciding if it is safe to ship, that was always the slow part. AI just made the first half nearly free and left the second half untouched.

So the math changes. If an agent produces a function that calls three APIs and touches a shared database table, someone still has to trace every one of those paths before it merges. That review doesn't get faster because the code got written faster.

A related post going around makes a similar point from a different angle: not every workflow needs an LLM sitting in the middle of it. Some tasks are better served by a plain script or a deterministic rule, precisely because the output is predictable and doesn't need a human to double check reasoning every time.

That's the actual design question. Before automating a workflow, it's worth asking whether the output will be easy to verify, or whether you're just moving the bottleneck from production to review.

A system that ships fast but can't be checked quickly isn't saving anyone time. It's shifting the cost to whoever has to sign off on it.

Where does review slow your team down right now, writing the code or trusting it?

topic: Mapping process before automating it
hook: Automation only scales the parts you already understand
caption:
Most automation projects fail before the first workflow goes live.

Not because of the tools.

Because nobody mapped the process first.

I see this constantly.

A business wants to automate lead follow-up.

But nobody can explain what actually happens between a form fill and a closed deal.

Who checks the lead.

What makes it qualified.

When someone gets a reply.

Why some leads sit for three days.

If you cannot explain the process in plain English, automating it just makes the mess move faster.

The fix is boring.

Write the current process down, step by step, before touching n8n or Zapier or any agent.

Then automate the steps that are actually repeatable.

Leave judgment calls to people until you trust the pattern.

What's one process in your business you've never actually written down step by step?

topic: Apple Building an AI Agent for Devices
subtopic: GTM & product strategy for agentic assistants
hook: Apple is reportedly building an agent that can control devices, browse, and code.
caption:
Apple is reportedly building an agent that can control devices, browse, and code.

A few outlets reported this within the same two hours, which tells you something on its own. This isn't a leaked roadmap item. It's a signal everyone noticed at once.

If it's accurate, it marks a shift. Agents stop being a thing developers wire together in n8n or a backend. They become a feature baked into the operating system your customers already use every day.

That changes expectations fast.

Right now, a lot of businesses treat "agent" as a selling point. Soon, it'll just be what people assume software does. The bar moves from "does this have AI" to "why does this still make me click five things manually."

A few things worth sitting with:

What actually makes something an agent, not just a feature with a chat window on it. Most of what gets called an agent today is a workflow with a language model bolted on. That's fine, but it's not the same thing as a system that holds context, takes action, and checks its own work.

The model was never the hard part. Orchestration is. Error handling, retries, knowing when to hand off to a human, that's the actual engineering. OS-level agents will make that more obvious, not less important.

Worth auditing now: where does your business still need a manual handoff between two systems that should talk to each other. That's usually where the real cost is sitting, not in whether you have the newest model.

What's the one manual handoff slowing your team down right now?

topic: AI Agents Outperforming Human Experts on Judgment Tasks
subtopic: Agent reasoning quality vs. professional judgment
hook: A recent KPMG audit trial reportedly found AI agents asking sharper, more probing questions than trained accountants reviewing the same files.
caption:
A recent KPMG audit trial reportedly found AI agents asking sharper, more probing questions than trained accountants reviewing the same files.

If that holds up, it says something uncomfortable about a lot of professional work.

The bottleneck usually isn't domain knowledge. Most trained professionals have that. The bottleneck is curiosity. Asking the question that doesn't fit the template. Noticing the number that's technically correct but still wrong.

An agent that's been given the right instructions and enough context can ask every question on the checklist, every time, without getting tired or protective of its own assumptions.

That's useful. It's also not the whole story.

Agents don't know when a question matters more than the checklist says it does. They don't carry the judgment that comes from having been burned by a bad assumption before. That's still a human job, at least for now.

Which is probably the actual lesson here. Not that agents replace judgment, but that they're good at the part of judgment that's really just discipline, consistency, and not skipping steps when you're tired or rushed.

Most businesses don't need an agent that thinks like a senior auditor. They need one that never forgets to ask the obvious question, with a human still reviewing what it finds.

Where do you think that line actually sits in your field?

topic: closing workflow gaps
hook: Most businesses don't need more tools, just fewer gaps
caption:
Nobody's workflow problem is a tools problem.

I see this every week.

A business has a CRM.
A calendar app.
An email tool.
A spreadsheet for tracking leads.

Every single tool works fine on its own.

The actual problem is the space between them.

Someone copies a lead from a form into the CRM.
Someone checks three places before a call.
Someone updates a sheet that nothing else reads.

That gap is where time disappears.

Not in the tools.
In the handoff between them.

When I build a workflow, I'm not adding another app to the stack.

I'm closing the gap between the ones already there.

Form fills in.
Data moves on its own.
The right person gets notified.
Nothing gets copied twice.

That's the whole job most of the time.

Not more software.
Less distance between the software you already pay for.

What's the gap in your workflow that nobody's closed yet?

topic: Governance Policies as a Precondition for Agent Autonomy
subtopic: Semantic/policy-based control layers before agents act
hook: Two platform vendors shipped agent governance tooling in the same week.
caption:
Two platform vendors shipped agent governance tooling in the same week.

Google added semantic policy controls. Oracle shipped MCP and A2A connection governance. Different companies, same underlying move.

The question is changing. It used to be: can the agent do this. Now it's: what checks run before it's allowed to try.

That shift matters more than it sounds.

Most agent setups right now rely on a human checking the output after the fact. Someone reviews the email before it sends, approves the record before it updates, checks the action before it fires. That works at low volume. It falls apart once an agent is running dozens of actions a day across multiple systems.

The pattern showing up across these new tools is different. Define what's allowed as policy, separate from the code that does the work. Evaluate the intent against that policy before execution, not after.

It's the same idea as role-based access control, just applied to agent behavior instead of user permissions. Nothing exotic. Just a layer that's been missing.

This is where agent projects usually stall. Not the model, not the tool calling. The part where someone has to decide, in advance, what the agent is actually allowed to touch and under what conditions.

If you're building agents into a real workflow, that policy layer is worth designing before you expand what the agent can do.

What's your approval process for agent actions right now? Still manual, or is any of it written down as policy?

topic: Semantic governance policies for AI agents
subtopic: Pre-action agent permission checks
hook: Google shipped semantic governance policies for AI agents this week. Same day, Citi told customers not to connect third-party AI agents to their accounts.
caption:
Google shipped semantic governance policies for AI agents this week. Same day, Citi told customers not to connect third-party AI agents to their accounts.

Different companies, same conclusion: letting an agent act first and reviewing later doesn't scale.

Most agent setups still work like this. The agent calls a tool, does the thing, and someone checks the logs afterward if something breaks. That's fine for a demo. It falls apart once an agent has real access to a calendar, a CRM, or a bank account.

What's changing is where the check happens. Instead of reviewing what an agent did, the platform now checks what it's about to do before it does it. Permission lives in the policy layer, not in the prompt and not in someone's memory of what the agent is allowed to touch.

This matters for anyone building agents into a real workflow. A guardrail you wrote into a system prompt is a suggestion. A guardrail enforced at the platform level is a rule the agent physically cannot break.

If you're putting an agent in front of customer data, payment systems, or anything with downside risk, the question isn't whether the agent is smart enough. It's whether there's a permission check sitting between the agent's decision and the action it's about to take.

That's the boring infrastructure work nobody shows in demos. It's also the part that decides whether an agent is safe to actually deploy.

topic: Automation ownership and maintenance
hook: Automation without ownership just moves the chaos faster
caption:
Most automation projects fail for a boring reason.

Nobody owns the workflow after it ships.

Here's what I mean.

A team connects their CRM to their email tool.
They add a Zapier step for lead routing.
They wire up a Slack notification.

It works for three weeks.

Then a field name changes in the CRM.
Or a plan upgrade shifts an API limit.
Or someone on the team starts using a new tag.

The workflow breaks quietly.

No error message anyone sees.
No alert in a channel people check.
Just leads sitting there, unrouted, for two weeks.

This is the part nobody talks about when they sell automation.

The build is maybe 30 percent of the work.

The other 70 percent is someone checking it, maintaining it, and treating it like a system with a pulse instead of a project that's done.

Speed without ownership just means your mess moves faster and breaks somewhere new.

What's one automation in your business that nobody actually checks on anymore?

topic: MCP and AI Tool Supply Chain Leaking Secrets
subtopic: Dependency risk in agentic tool ecosystems
hook: An AI agent is only as careful as the weakest connector it talks to.
caption:
An AI agent is only as careful as the weakest connector it talks to.

Most businesses think about AI risk at the model level. Is it hallucinating, is it biased, is it saying something wrong. That's the wrong layer to worry about right now.

The real risk is the supply chain around the agent.

MCP made it simple to plug an agent into mail, CRM, drive, issue trackers, anything with an API. Every one of those connections is a small trust decision. You're not just trusting the AI vendor anymore. You're trusting whoever built that connector, however they chose to store credentials, and whatever permissions they asked for.

Independent security research this year has been pointing at the same pattern. Credentials get stored in local config files. Setup instructions often involve pasting in a string that contains the actual keys. Anyone can publish a connector, so the bar for getting into an agent's toolset is low.

The part worth sitting with: a lot of these connectors are opaque. You can see that an agent has access to a mail or CRM connector, but not always what that connector actually does with the data it touches, or who maintains it.

That's the gap. Not the model. The thing standing between the model and your systems.

If you're building or buying agentic workflows, the useful exercise isn't asking what the AI can do. It's asking what every connector in that stack can reach, and whether anyone has actually looked at how it handles credentials.

Treat each connector like a vendor you're onboarding, not a feature you're switching on.

If you're not sure what your agent's connector list actually has access to right now, that's worth checking before adding the next one.

What's the most repetitive part of your workflow right now, and how many tools does it already touch?

topic: AI Research Capability Creep Into Hard Sciences
subtopic: LLMs assisting with unsolved math and physics problems
hook: Claude just contributed to progress on a Riemann hypothesis proof and a black hole physics problem.
caption:
Claude just contributed to progress on a Riemann hypothesis proof and a black hole physics problem.

Not writing code. Not summarizing papers. Actually moving open research problems forward.

This is a different category of task than what most people associate with AI agents right now.

Most business use cases are still pattern-matching work. Draft this email. Classify this lead. Pull data from this system and put it in that one. Useful, but bounded. The system knows what a good answer looks like before it starts.

Research math and physics don't work that way. Nobody knows what the right answer looks like in advance. The model has to reason through something genuinely unsolved, and a human has to check whether what came back actually holds up.

That gap between "the model generated something" and "a person confirmed it's correct" is the part worth paying attention to.

It's the same gap that matters in business automation, just with lower stakes. An agent that drafts a contract clause, qualifies a lead, or restructures customer data still needs a checkpoint where a person looks at the output before it goes anywhere important.

The interesting shift isn't that AI can now do more. It's that the harder the problem, the more deliberate the human checkpoint needs to be, not less.

Where are you still relying on a person to catch mistakes your AI tools could be making quietly?

topic: Data quality in automation
hook: Most automations fail at the data, not the logic
caption:
Everyone debugs the wrong part of their workflow.

Here's what I mean.

A workflow breaks.
First instinct: check the logic.
Rewrite the steps.
Add more conditions.

But nine times out of ten, the logic was fine.

The real problem was upstream.

A field that's sometimes empty.
A date format that changes between tools.
A lead with no email, just a phone number.
A webhook that fires twice.

Your automation isn't reasoning wrong.
It's reasoning on bad input.

So before you touch the workflow steps, look at what's actually flowing into them.

Where does the data get messy.
Where does it get duplicated.
Where does it arrive incomplete.

Clean the input and half your 'logic problems' disappear on their own.

What's the messiest data source feeding one of your workflows right now?

topic: Airlines Blocking Third-Party AI Agents From Booking Travel
subtopic: Platform access restrictions for agentic AI
hook: An airline just blocked third-party AI agents from booking or managing flights on a customer's behalf.
caption:
An airline just blocked third-party AI agents from booking or managing flights on a customer's behalf.

No partner program, no API exception for agent traffic. If the request looks like it's coming from an agent instead of a person, it gets refused.

This is worth paying attention to, not because it's about travel, but because of what it signals.

Agentic AI doesn't run on capability alone. It runs on permission. A model can be fully capable of completing a task and still get blocked, because the platform on the other end decides who is allowed to act and who isn't.

We've seen this pattern before. Platforms open APIs, then tighten them once automated traffic starts affecting their business, their data, or their ability to upsell a human in the loop. Travel, ticketing, retail checkouts, even some CRMs have all moved this direction at different points.

The practical implication for anyone building agent workflows: the risk usually isn't whether the agent can do the task. It's whether the platform on the other end will keep letting it.

That changes how you design things. Official APIs and documented integrations age a lot better than workarounds built on scraping a UI or mimicking browser behavior. Workarounds get shut off fast, and usually without warning.

If you're building or relying on an agent right now, it's worth asking a plain question: what access is this depending on, and who controls it?

What's a workflow in your business that depends on access you don't actually control?

topic: Automation copies broken processes
hook: Automation copies your current process, good or bad
caption:
Most automation projects fail before a single workflow runs.

Here's why.

Teams map out their messy process.
Then they automate the mess.

Now it just runs faster.

I see this constantly with lead handoffs.
Sales forgets to update the CRM.
Marketing sends leads with no context.
Follow-up happens whenever someone remembers.

Automate that exact flow and you get the same gaps.
Just quicker and with less visibility into where it broke.

The fix isn't more tools.

It's fixing the process first.

Write down what should happen.
Not what currently happens.

Then build the system around that.

What's one step in your process you'd actually redesign before automating it?

topic: Claude Ship Automates PR Review and Fixes
subtopic: AI agents closing the loop on code review
hook: Anthropic just automated the one checkpoint teams never automated.
caption:
Anthropic shipped a tool that has an agent review pull requests and apply the fixes itself.

That's a different kind of automation than what most teams have been dealing with.

Writing code was never the hard part to automate. Review was the checkpoint teams kept for a reason. Someone had to look at the diff and decide if it was safe to merge.

Now that decision is on the table too.

This isn't the same question as "will the handoff between two tools break." It's "am I comfortable letting something else make the call on what's good enough to ship."

That's not a reliability problem. It's a judgment problem.

Most businesses thinking about agents jump straight to "what task can this replace." The more useful question is "what decision am I actually handing over."

Tasks are easy to automate and easy to check. Decisions are where things get expensive if you get it wrong, and expensive to walk back once a team gets used to not checking.

If you're building or adopting agents right now, the review step is a good place to ask that question before it gets asked for you.

Where does judgment, not just task execution, slow your team down right now?

topic: Claude Ship automates the last mile of software delivery
subtopic: AI-assisted development
hook: Writing code was never the slow part for most teams.
caption:
Writing code was never the slow part for most teams.

The slow part is everything after: opening a PR, waiting on review, fixing comments, waiting again, merging, shipping.

Anthropic's new Claude Ship is aimed at that stretch. Not generating code, but moving it through review, fixes, and deployment with less manual back and forth.

That's a different problem than what most AI coding tools have targeted. Copilot and the first wave of agentic coding assistants focused on getting code written faster. The bottleneck just moved downstream, into review queues and release cycles.

If Claude Ship actually closes that gap, the interesting shift isn't "AI writes code now." It's that the last mile of software delivery, the part full of waiting and handoffs, becomes something a system can own with a human checking the output instead of producing every step of it.

That matters for small teams especially. A lot of them don't have a dedicated release engineer. The PR sits there because everyone is busy, not because the code is bad.

Worth watching whether this holds up once it's running against real production pipelines instead of demos. Shipping software has more edge cases than writing it.

What's eating more time on your team right now, writing the code or getting it through review and out the door?

topic: Automation edge case failures
hook: Most automations fail at the edges, not the middle
caption:
Nobody talks about the boring part of automation.

The middle always works.

You map the steps, connect the tools, test it once, it runs clean.

Then three weeks later it breaks.

Not because the logic was wrong.

Because of the edge case nobody planned for.

A lead with no last name.

A date formatted differently than expected.

An API that returns an empty array instead of null.

These aren't dramatic failures. They're quiet ones.

The workflow just stops, or worse, it keeps going with bad data.

This is why I spend more time on error handling than on the happy path.

The happy path is easy. Anyone can build that in an afternoon.

The edges are where the real engineering is.

What's the weirdest edge case that broke one of your systems?

topic: Agent-run sandboxes testing their own containment
subtopic: AI agent reliability and oversight boundaries
hook: Anthropic built a test to catch its own AI trying to escape its sandbox.
caption:
Anthropic built an internal test called Siren to check whether their own models try to break out of an insecure sandbox.

That detail matters more than the headline.

A company that trains these models is treating containment as something to verify, not something to assume. If they test for it, you should too, especially once an agent has real tool access instead of just answering questions in a chat window.

Most businesses deploying agents right now skip this step entirely. They give an agent access to a CRM, an inbox, a database, or a file system, and they assume it will stay inside the lines because the instructions say so.

Instructions are not a boundary. They're a suggestion the model is free to reinterpret under pressure.

A few things worth taking from this:

Permissions should be a deliberate design decision. What can this agent actually touch, and what happens if it tries to go further.

Logging is not optional. If you can't see what the agent attempted, you can't catch the moments it tried something outside scope.

Unusual behavior under load or edge cases is a signal, not a bug to shrug off. That's exactly when containment gets tested in production, whether you planned for it or not.

Before an agent touches real systems, its boundary should be tested the same way you'd test any other failure mode. Not because the agent is untrustworthy, but because untested assumptions are how small mistakes turn into real damage.

What's the most generous permission you've given an AI agent so far, and did you actually test what happens if it tries to go past it?

topic: AI agents acting on behalf of their vendor, not the user
subtopic: Trust and incentive alignment in agentic products
hook: Banks are warning customers that they bear liability when an AI agent makes a mistake on their behalf.
caption:
Banks are warning customers that they bear liability when an AI agent makes a mistake on their behalf.

That warning is worth sitting with.

An agent embedded in a product is built by the company that built the product. It is optimized for that company's goals first. Retention, upsell, platform lock-in, whatever the business model rewards. The user's actual outcome is a secondary constraint, not the objective function.

Most people treat autonomous features as neutral infrastructure. Like a calculator or a spreadsheet formula. Something that just executes your intent faithfully.

But an agent isn't neutral. It has a system prompt you didn't write, guardrails you didn't choose, and incentives set by someone else's roadmap.

That makes it a vendor relationship, not a feature.

And vendor relationships need the same questions you'd ask before signing any contract. Who is liable when it's wrong. What data does it have access to. Who benefits when it takes an action you didn't explicitly approve.

If a business is putting agents into real workflows, the useful question isn't "can it act autonomously." It's "whose interests is it acting on, and what happens when that's unclear."

Human approval on consequential actions isn't a limitation. It's the line where accountability stays with the business instead of quietly shifting to a vendor's terms of service.

topic: automation failure points at handoffs
hook: Most automations fail at the handoff nobody designed for
caption:
Nobody plans for the gap between two systems.

They plan for the systems.

I see this constantly when I audit a client's workflow.

The CRM works fine.
The email tool works fine.
The form works fine.

Then someone built a manual step between them years ago and forgot about it.

A person checking a spreadsheet.
A person copying a lead into another tool.
A person approving something in a Slack message that nobody else sees.

That step becomes invisible because it works, until the person goes on holiday or changes roles.

Then the whole workflow quietly stops and nobody notices for a week.

When I design a workflow now, I spend more time on the handoffs than the tools themselves.

What happens when a field is empty.
What happens when an API times out.
What happens when two records almost match but not quite.

The tools rarely fail.

The space between them does.

Where does your workflow actually break, at the tool level or at the handoff between two people or systems?

topic: Claude Skills now exposed over MCP
subtopic: Agent tool architecture
hook: Every agent project I look at has the same folder somewhere. Prompt_v2_final. Tool_configs_copy.
caption:
Every agent project I look at has the same folder somewhere. Prompt_v2_final. Tool_configs_copy. A pile of instructions one person wrote for one client, that nobody else can reuse without opening the file and rewriting half of it.

Anthropic just moved Claude Skills onto MCP, in public beta.

That sounds like a protocol update. It is actually a packaging change.

Right now, most teams building with Claude Code treat skills as prompt files sitting inside a project. Useful once, forgotten once the project ships. If another team wants the same capability, they rebuild it from scratch, slightly differently, with its own bugs.

Putting skills on MCP means a skill can be defined once and exposed as something other agents and other projects can call, the same way MCP already lets a model reach a database or an API. Instead of copying a prompt into a new repo, you point a new agent at the skill.

That is the real shift. Not smarter prompts. Shareable ones.

It does not remove the need for oversight. A portable skill still needs someone checking what it is allowed to touch and what happens when it fails. Packaging a capability so it travels well is different from trusting it to run unsupervised.

Teams that start treating skills like components, versioned, documented, reused on purpose, are going to spend a lot less time rebuilding the same logic for every new client or project.

What's the one prompt or tool setup you've rebuilt more than twice this year?

If you're building something similar, happy to compare architectures.

topic: CRM handoffs over more features
hook: Most CRMs don't need more fields, they need fewer handoffs
caption:
Your CRM is not the problem.

The handoffs are.

I keep seeing teams add more fields, more tags, more custom properties to a CRM that's already struggling.

But the lead isn't getting lost because a field is missing.

It's getting lost between the form, the inbox, the spreadsheet, and the person who finally updates the record three days later.

follow-up slows down

context gets dropped

someone forgets to update the next tool

One workflow I'd rather build than another dashboard:

form submission routes straight into qualification logic, qualification pushes into the CRM automatically, and the right person gets notified the moment it matters.

No copy-paste. No "I'll update that later."

The CRM isn't the system. It's just where the system ends up.

Where's the handoff in your process that still happens by hand?

topic: Google Forcing Workspace Agents Through Its Own MCP, With Missing Core Functions

This matters for anyone building agent workflows on top of a platform's own MCP implementation. You're not building on what the brand promises. You're building on whatever functions actually show up in the tool list.

I've seen the same pattern with CRM and calendar integrations long before MCP existed. The API documentation says one thing. The actual scopes and endpoints available say another.

So before wiring an agent to any MCP server, Workspace or otherwise, the first step isn't architecture. It's reading the tool list line by line and checking what's actually callable.

If you're working with MCP right now, what have you found missing that you expected to be there?

topic: Agent Compute Allocation Inside Labs
subtopic: Agents managing their own research infrastructure
hook: DeepMind is reportedly letting an AI agent make partial decisions about how compute gets allocated across its own experiments.
caption:
DeepMind is reportedly letting an AI agent make partial decisions about how compute gets allocated across its own experiments.

That is a different kind of autonomy than what most people picture when they hear "AI agent."

Most agent demos show a model answering questions or completing a task inside a chat window. This is a model making resource-level calls inside an internal process, the kind of decision that used to sit with a researcher or an ops team.

The gap between those two things is the whole story right now.

In business automation, this is the same line I think about with every workflow. An agent that drafts a follow-up email is low risk. An agent that decides which lead gets priority, which invoice gets flagged, or which task gets resourced first is a different category entirely.

The tools to build that second category already exist. The harder part is deciding where human approval still belongs before the agent gets that kind of authority.

Where do you draw that line in your own workflows, at the task level or the resource level?

hook: Most automations fail at the handoff, not the task
caption:
Nobody talks about the boring part of automation.

Everyone wants to show the flashy workflow.

The AI step.
The trigger.
The fancy integration diagram.

But the part that actually breaks a system is the handoff.

Data moving from one tool to another.
A field that doesn't map the same way twice.
A status update that depends on a human clicking the right button at the right time.

The task itself is usually easy.

Summarize this.
Qualify this lead.
Update this record.

That part works in a demo every time.

What breaks production systems is the seam between steps.

Who owns the data once it leaves tool A.
What happens if tool B is slow to respond.
What the next step assumes was already true.

I spend more time designing handoffs than I do picking models or writing prompts.

That's the unglamorous work nobody posts about.

It's also the work that decides if a system survives past week one.

Where does your workflow usually break, at the task or at the handoff?

topic: Duplicate Tool Calls After Timeouts in AI Agents
subtopic: Agent reliability engineering
hook: A timeout does not mean the tool call failed. It means the agent stopped waiting.
caption:
A timeout does not mean the tool call failed. It means the agent stopped waiting.

That distinction is where a lot of agent builds break once they leave the demo stage.

Here is the common failure mode. An agent calls a tool to charge a card, send an email, or book a slot. The response takes too long. The agent times out, assumes the call failed, and tries again. Except the first call went through. Now the customer is charged twice, or the email went out twice, or the same slot got booked twice.

The agent didn't make a reasoning mistake. It made a state mistake. It had no way to know whether the first attempt succeeded.

Backend engineers solved this problem years ago for payment systems. Every request gets an idempotency key. The receiving system checks if it has already seen that key before acting on it. If it has, it returns the original result instead of doing the work again.

Agents need the same pattern. Not better prompting, not a retry limit, an actual key tied to the action and a record of what state that action is in.

This has to live in the tool layer. You can tell a model to "be careful not to duplicate actions" and it will still duplicate actions, because the model has no memory of what happened on the other side of a dropped connection. The system calling the tool has to track that, not the prompt.

It is an unglamorous fix for an unglamorous problem. But it is usually the difference between an agent that looks good in a demo and one a team is willing to trust with real transactions.

What's the riskiest tool call in your agent right now?

topic: Who Is Accountable When AI Agents Make Costly Mistakes
subtopic: budget and permission accountability for autonomous agents
hook: An agent can book travel, send a refund, or sign off on a lease. The question nobody answers upfront is who owns it when that action goes wrong.
caption:
An agent can book travel, send a refund, or sign off on a lease. The question nobody answers upfront is who owns it when that action goes wrong.

Most agent rollouts focus on what the agent can do. Fewer teams define who is accountable for what it does, and what ceiling it operates under before it acts.

That gap shows up fast once agents touch money or legal commitments. A support agent that overpromises a refund is annoying. An agent that signs a contract or gives a tenant wrong information about their lease is a different category of problem, and "the AI did it" is not an answer anyone accepts after the fact.

The fix isn't more capability. It's structure around the capability.

A named owner for each agent. A spend or action ceiling set in advance. Clear rules for what requires human sign-off versus what the agent can clear on its own. Logging that shows why it made the call it made.

This is the same discipline businesses already apply to employees with purchasing authority or signing authority. Nobody gives a new hire an unlimited expense account on day one. Agents need the same boundaries, and right now most companies skip straight to deployment without setting them.

The interesting part of agentic AI was never really the model. It's the governance wrapped around it, and that part gets built by people, not prompts.

If you're putting an agent into production this quarter, the accountability question is worth answering before the capability question.

caption:

The handoff to the human or the next tool is where it quietly breaks.

A lead gets scored but never reaches sales.

Good automation design spends more time on the handoff than the task itself.

Who receives this.
What happens if they don't act.
How does the system know it actually worked.

The task is the easy 20 percent.
